name: VPC, VPN and Private Networking
intent: Decide who can reach whom in a cloud network by reading route tables, gateways and peering, and avoid the over-open default.
scenario: A VPC 10.0.0.0/16 has a public subnet with a web server, a private subnet with an app server and a database subnet. A NAT gateway serves the private subnet; a peer VPC, an on-premises network over a VPN and the internet are outside. The toy evaluator answers 'can A reach B?' for each pair.
problem: In a cloud network nothing is reachable because of a cable; it is reachable because a route table says so and a gateway agrees. The words 'public' and 'private' name a routing choice, not a place. A route that looks right can still fail: a NAT gateway with no route in the private subnet, peering with a route on only one side, two networks that use the same address range, or a database subnet that got a default route to the internet 'just to download a patch'. Seeing the network as lookups makes these failures easy to find.

howItWorks.title: A subnet is public or private because of its route table
howItWorks.text: Every subnet is associated with a route table, a list of destination CIDRs and targets. A route to the internet gateway (0.0.0.0/0 to igw) makes a subnet public, and its hosts reach the internet only if they also have a public IP. A subnet without that route is private. The local route (the VPC's own CIDR) is always present and cannot be removed, so everything inside the VPC can reach everything else unless a security group or ACL says no.

howItWorks.title: Longest prefix wins
howItWorks.text: For each packet the router picks, among the routes whose CIDR contains the destination, the one with the longest prefix (the most specific). A /16 for the peer VPC beats the /0 default. A route to 192.168.0.0/16 via the VPN sends on-premises traffic there even when a default route to the NAT gateway exists. No matching route means the packet is dropped, which looks like a timeout (see CIDR and subnetting).

howItWorks.title: NAT gateway versus internet gateway
howItWorks.text: An internet gateway translates for hosts that have a public IP, and accepts traffic from the internet to them. A NAT gateway lets private hosts start connections out: it sits in a public subnet, swaps the private source for its own public address and drops unsolicited inbound packets. A private subnet's default route should point at the NAT gateway. If the route is missing the app in the sample loses the internet (no route) and every update or external API call fails. Neither gateway delivers private (RFC 1918) destinations to the internet: a packet for 10.1.0.10 that follows a default route out is dropped.

howItWorks.title: Peering needs distinct CIDRs and a route on both sides
howItWorks.text: VPC peering connects two VPCs privately. Each side must add a route to the other's CIDR through the peering connection; the toy model shows a one-sided setup where the request leaves and the reply has no way back, so connections hang. Peering is not transitive and the two address ranges must not overlap: with both VPCs on 10.0.0.0/16 the peering cannot be created, and the destination 10.0.0.10 matches the local route, so traffic goes to a host that does not exist here.

howItWorks.title: VPN and private links reach on-premises networks
howItWorks.text: A site-to-site VPN builds an encrypted tunnel over the internet to your data centre; a dedicated private link (such as Direct Connect or ExpressRoute) uses a leased circuit with more predictable latency. Either way, you add a route for the on-premises CIDR (for example 192.168.0.0/16) to the gateway, and the far side must route replies back. Every address range you connect needs to be distinct, so plan CIDRs before the first VPC is created.

howItWorks.title: The over-open default
howItWorks.text: The cheapest way to make a failing connection work is to add 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway and give the host a public IP. In the sample the database subnet is then reachable from the internet (the working path count rises and 'internet to db' flips from no path to reachable). Routing is the first gate and security groups the second; relying on only one, and widening both at once to debug, is how databases end up on the public internet.

pros: Private subnets keep databases and internal services off the internet by construction, not by firewall rules alone
Route tables make reachability explicit and reviewable: the answer to 'can A reach B' is a lookup
Peering, VPN and private links connect networks without exposing them publicly
NAT gives private hosts outbound access with no inbound exposure
cons: Address planning is permanent: overlapping CIDRs block peering and VPN and are painful to renumber
NAT gateways cost money per hour and per gigabyte, and are a shared bottleneck and port limit
Peering is not transitive, so many VPCs need a hub (such as a transit gateway) or many connections
Failures are silent: a missing route or one-way route shows up as a timeout
whenToUse: Putting databases, caches and internal services in private subnets with no route to the internet gateway
A NAT gateway (or, for IPv6, an egress-only internet gateway) per environment for outbound updates and API calls from private hosts
Peering or a transit gateway between VPCs with distinct CIDRs; VPN or a private link to data centres
Private endpoints for managed services, so traffic to them never leaves the provider network
whenNotToUse: Giving a database a public IP and a route to the internet gateway for convenience or debugging
Starting every VPC at 10.0.0.0/16: pick distinct ranges per environment and region from the start
Using a VPN or peering as a security boundary on its own: connected networks still need security groups
Sending heavy outbound traffic through a NAT gateway when a private endpoint would avoid the per-gigabyte cost
pitfalls: Public subnet without a public IP: the route exists but the internet gateway only serves hosts that have a public address
NAT gateway placed in a private subnet, or the private route table missing the NAT default route: outbound traffic has no way out
One-way peering: the route exists on one side only, so requests arrive and replies are dropped
Overlapping CIDRs with a peer or on-premises network: the more specific or local route wins and traffic goes to the wrong place
Assuming peering is transitive: A to B and B to C does not give A to C
Adding 0.0.0.0/0 and a public IP to a database subnet to make a patch download work, and leaving it there
Debugging only security groups: a missing route fails before any rule is evaluated

roles.label: Host
roles.description: An instance in a subnet that sends or receives packets.

roles.label: Route table
roles.description: The list of destinations and targets that decides where a packet goes; longest prefix wins.

roles.label: Gateway
roles.description: The internet gateway, NAT gateway, peering connection or VPN that carries traffic across a boundary.

roles.label: Remote network
roles.description: The internet, a peer VPC or an on-premises network.

quiz.question: An app server in a private subnet cannot download updates. Its route table has only the local route. What is missing?
options: A public IP address on the app server
A default route (0.0.0.0/0) to a NAT gateway that sits in a public subnet
A default route to the internet gateway from the private subnet
A peering connection to the public subnet
quiz.explanation: A private subnet reaches the internet through a NAT gateway placed in a public subnet. Pointing the private subnet straight at the internet gateway would not work without a public IP, and it would make the host publicly exposed.

quiz.question: VPC A (10.0.0.0/16) and VPC B (10.0.0.0/16) are to be connected. What is the most useful action?
options: Add routes on both sides and use the more specific one
Peer them and rely on security groups to separate the hosts
Renumber one VPC to a distinct range before connecting them
Put a NAT gateway between them
quiz.explanation: Overlapping ranges cannot be peered, and the local route would capture the traffic anyway. Distinct CIDRs are a precondition for peering, VPN and transit connections, so renumbering (or translating at the edge) is required.

quiz.question: Peering is set up and a route to VPC B exists in VPC A. Requests to B hang. Which check comes first?
options: Whether B's route table has a route back to A's CIDR through the peering connection
Whether the NAT gateway has run out of ports
Whether B has a public IP address
Whether the peering connection uses TLS
quiz.explanation: Peering needs a route on both sides. If only A has one, requests arrive but replies have nowhere to go, which looks like a hang. Public IPs and NAT are not involved in a private peering path.
